entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Emperor Xuan of Han, born Liu Bingyi (劉病已), was the tenth emperor of the Han dynasty, reigning from 74 to 48 BC, and was one of the only four Western Han emperors to receive a temple name. During his reign, the Han dynasty prospered economically and militarily became a regional superpower of the Far East, with significant trade networks stretching from China to Central Asia and Korea. The capital city of Chang'an (modern-day Xi'an) experienced unprecedented growth, with a population of over 1 million people and a vast array of cultural, artistic, and intellectual achievements.

His reign, along with that of his great-uncle and predecessor Emperor Zhao, are known by historians as the Zhaoxuan Restoration, a period of significant cultural and economic achievements that solidified the Han dynasty's position as a major power in the ancient world. The emperor's court attracted scholars, poets, and artists from across the empire, including the famous historian Sima Qian, who would later become one of the most influential chroniclers of Chinese history.

The legacy of Emperor Xuan of Han can be seen in the numerous archaeological sites and museums that dot the Chinese countryside, including the famous Terracotta Army, which was first discovered in 1974 and has since become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

One of the most striking legacies of Emperor Xuan of Han is the extensive network of roads and highways that he built, including the famous Silk Road, which connected China to Central Asia and the Mediterranean region. This network played a crucial role in the exchange of goods, ideas, and cultures between East Asia and the wider world.

The impact of Emperor Xuan of Han's reign can also be seen in the numerous historical records and literary works that he commissioned, including the famous 'Shiji' (Records of the Historian) by Sima Qian, which remains one of the most important sources of ancient Chinese history.
